dervis-irab:1-4.t:
* I'rab:
(لِإِيلافِ قُرَيْشٍ) The statements of the parsers and exegetes about what this lām, which opens the sūra, is attached to have been greatly confused, so much so that we cannot decide on a conclusive statement; but we shall choose the view we incline to, and then cite for you some of the statements of the parsers, because they spent all their scholarly energies and mental faculties on directing this attachment. We say: (لإيلاف) is attached to His later saying (فليعبدوا), as if He had said: "If they do not worship Allah for all His abundant, successive blessings, then let them worship Him for their being accustomed to the winter and summer journey", which is an abundant blessing that enabled them to trade and guaranteed them an easy livelihood. (إيلاف) is the maṣdar of ālafa, a quadriliteral verb of the pattern akrama; one says ālaftuhu ulifuhu īlāfan. The Quraysh had two journeys: in winter they travelled to Yemen and in summer to Syria, where they obtained provisions and traded. On both journeys they were secure, because they were the people of Allah's sanctuary and the custodians of His House, so people stood in awe of them and none molested them, whereas other traders and caravan-owners were exposed to dangers and people snatched them away. You say ālaftu l-makān ulifuhu īlāfan when you are familiar with the place, so I am a mūlif. He said:
شددت إليك الرحيل فوق شملة ... من المؤلفات الرهو غير الأوارك
(I fastened the saddle for travelling to you upon a swift she-camel, one of those accustomed to the easy gait, not of those that stay in the arāk pastures.)
Al-shimlāl, with shadda, is the light she-camel, swift in her going; that is, I fastened the saddle upon a swift she-camel, going to you; that she-camel is among the she-camels accustomed to al-rahw, i.e., the easy, straight pace. It is also transmitted as al-zahw with zāy, which is their pace after coming to water. Al-awārik is the plural of ārika, those that stay in the place of the arāk tree, grazing on it, or grazing another plant called al-ḥamḍ. The meaning is: my she-camel is not like that; rather she is fed with fodder and prepared for travel. This view that we have chosen is attributed to al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, and that is enough for you. Al-Zamakhsharī cited it among the views he cited and began with it, but there is an objection to it, namely the entry of the fāʾ on (فليعبدوا). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say, 'Why did the fāʾ enter?' I say: because of the sense of condition in the sentence, for the meaning is: 'if they will not [worship Him for all His blessings], then let them worship Him for this one, which is a manifest blessing.'" Al-Shihāb al-Samīn began with his statement: "There are several views on what this verse is attached to:
First, that it is attached to what precedes it in the previous sūra, His saying (فَجَعَلَهُمْ كَعَصْفٍ مَأْكُولٍ). Al-Zamakhsharī said: this is like taḍmīn (enjambment) in poetry, which is that the meaning of a verse is connected to the one before it in a way that is sound only with it. In the codex of Ubayy the two are a single sūra without separation, and from ʿUmar it is reported that he recited them both in the second rakʿa of the Maghrib prayer, having recited sūrat al-Tīn in the first. Abū l-Ḥasan al-Akhfash held this view, except that al-Ḥawfī said: a group rejected this view, because if it were so, (لإيلاف) would be part of the sūra (أَلَمْ تَرَ), and the consensus of all on separating the two indicates otherwise." I say: the scholars of rhetoric and the early critics of poetry agreed that taḍmīn is among the faults of poetry, so how can the recitation be taken on it, when the style of the Qur'an is too eloquent for criticism and censure to reach it? It was also said that it is attached to an omitted (أعجبوا) ("marvel!"); this view may offer relief from positing implied elements and interpretation. Just as the parsers differed in the parsing, so the reciters differed in the readings, for which the longer works should be consulted. As for Ibn Khālawayh, he said: "It is the maṣdar of ālafa yūlifu īlāfan, so he is mūlif, like āmana yūminu īmānan, so he is mūmin. Whoever read (إلفهم) made it a maṣdar of alifa yaʾlafu ilfan, so he is ālif, like ʿalima yaʿlamu ʿilman, so he is ʿālim. The imperative from the lengthened form is ālif, O Zayd, and from the short form ilaf, O Zayd. The scholars differed about (لإيلاف). A group said it and (ألم تر) are one sūra, among them al-Farrāʾ and Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna; both said: the implied form is 'He made them like eaten straw for the Ilāf of Quraysh'; on this basis the lām is the lām of genitive case connected with (ألم تر). Al-Khalīl and the Basrans said: the lām is the lām of annexation connected with (فليعبدوا), the implied form being: 'let them worship the Lord of this House because He favoured them with the Ilāf of Quraysh and turned from them the evil of the Companions of the Elephant.' Ibn Mujāhid related to me from al-Summarī from al-Farrāʾ that he said: it is permissible for the lām to be the lām of wonder, as if He said: 'Marvel at Muḥammad for the Ilāf of Quraysh', as the poet, al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī, said:
أتخذل ناصري وتعزّ عبسا ... أيربوع بن غيظ للمعنّي
(Will you forsake my helper and honour ʿAbs? O Yarbūʿ ibn Ghayẓ — [marvel] for the afflicted one!)
meaning: marvel for the afflicted one."
(قريش) is a muḍāf ilayhi. It is a tribe tracing back to al-Naḍr ibn Kināna; they were named by the diminutive of al-qirsh, a great creature in the sea that plays havoc with ships and can be overcome only with fire. It is reported that Muʿāwiya asked Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, "Why was Quraysh so named?" He said: "After a sea creature that eats and is not eaten, that rises above and is not risen above", and he recited:
وقريش هي التي تسكن البح ... ر بها سمّيت قريش قريشا
تأكل الغثّ والسمين ولا تت ... رك يوم لذي جناحين ريشا ولهم آخر الزمان نبي ... يكثر القتل فيهم والخموشا
(Quraysh is the one that dwells in the sea; by it Quraysh was named Quraysh. / It eats the lean and the fat, and leaves not for any winged creature a feather. And at the end of time they will have a prophet, among whom killing and scratching [wounds] will increase.)
Ibn Khālawayh said: It is also said that they were called Quraysh from the clashing (taqāruš) of spears. The diminutive is for magnification. It is also said that it is from al-qarsh, meaning earning, because they earned through their trade and travel across the lands. Quraysh is declined fully (ṣurifat) because the clan (al-ḥayy) is intended; had the tribe been intended it would be a diptote. Sībawayh said of Maʿadd, Thaqīf, Quraysh and Kināna: these are more often for clans, though to treat them as names of tribes is permissible and good. (إِيلافِهِمْ رِحْلَةَ الشِّتاءِ وَالصَّيْفِ) (إيلافهم) is a badal (substitute) for (لإيلاف), a restricted substitute for an unrestricted one: the Ilāf is left unrestricted in the first and restricted in the second by the winter and summer journeys, to magnify the matter of the Ilāf and to remind of the abundant blessings. The hāʾ is muḍāf ilayhi, and (رحلة الشتاء والصيف) is the direct object of (إيلافهم) because it is a maṣdar. [Translator's note: at this point the Arabic text of the source runs on without a break: "لأنه مصدرَلْيَعْبُدُوا رَبَّ هذَا الْبَيْتِ)", so the end of this passage and the opening of the next verse's heading are fused; the text appears defective here. The sentence after this point concerns the verse (فَلْيَعْبُدُوا رَبَّ هذَا الْبَيْتِ).] (فَلْيَعْبُدُوا رَبَّ هذَا الْبَيْتِ) The fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ because it occurs in the apodosis of an implied condition. The lām is the lām of command, and (يعبدوا) is an imperfect verb jussive by the lām; the wāw is the fāʿil; (رب) is the direct object; (هذا) is muḍāf ilayhi; and (البيت) is a badal from (هذا). Ibn Khālawayh parsed it as an adjective, but I do not like that, even though the grammarians said it. I think that a non-derived noun after a demonstrative cannot be parsed as an adjective at all; the better course is that the derived noun be the adjective and the non-derived a badal. (الَّذِي أَطْعَمَهُمْ مِنْ جُوعٍ وَآمَنَهُمْ مِنْ خَوْفٍ) (الذي) is an adjective of (رب) or a badal from it; the clause (أطعمهم) is a ṣila with no grammatical position; (من جوع) is attached to (أطعمهم); and (من) is causal, meaning: He favoured them and fed them to remove hunger from them, so a muḍāf must be implied, i.e., "for the sake of it". Likewise (آمنهم من خوف).
